Chapter 43

Settings: keys you can never read back

A key shown once, revoke rather than delete, and a saved view that stores the range as it was written.

By the end of this chapter

Build the settings that only matter after something has gone wrong.

Only the prefix is stored in clear, so the list can show sxt_a1b2c3d4… next to "created three weeks ago, last used four minutes ago" without any row being a live credential.

A system that can show you a key again is one where the key is readable at rest

Which makes a database backup a fleet compromise. Returning the clear value once, from the call that mints it, is not a usability compromise — it is the property that makes every other control meaningful.

Revoke, not delete

Deleting the row removes the record that a key existed at all — which is precisely the record somebody wants during an incident review, when the question is "what was this thing and who made it".

A range stored as it was written

A saved view of "the last six hours" must mean the last six hours when it is opened, not the six hours that happened to be current when it was saved. Storing two timestamps would make every saved view a historical snapshot — a different and much less useful feature.

The same distinction appears in the range picker: a relative range is *live* and says so, and "pin" is the deliberate act that freezes it into two timestamps. A link to "the last hour" means something different tomorrow, and the interface has to make that visible rather than surprising.

And the role each action needs

Reading the key list is admin, because knowing which integrations exist is itself worth restricting. Creating an alert rule is member, because a read-only viewer must not be able to page the whole team at three in the morning. Deleting one is admin, because it removes a safety net silently and the person who notices is whoever was relying on it during an incident.

What was typed before the page woke up

The read API’s end-to-end tests mint their keys through this form, straight after the page loads. On the phone profile, under load, one of them typed the key’s name a few dozen milliseconds before the bundle hydrated — and hydration emptied the field, the required check stopped the submission without a request ever leaving the browser, and no key appeared. The trace showed it plainly: fill finished, the remote queries a hydrated page makes went out a few dozen milliseconds later, and at the very next action the input’s value was an empty string.

The fix is the comparison Svelte already makes for bind:value — what is in the control now against what the server rendered — applied to the controls a remote form spreads its fields onto. It runs in the page’s <script>, which is the one moment that is both after the server’s HTML arrived and before the template hydrates over it.

The explore page has the other server-rendered field somebody types into, the name a view is saved under, and asks for the same thing from the same place: its script, which runs before the template is hydrated.

The select is the worse half. An emptied name at least stops the form; a read scope chosen before hydration comes back as ingest and submits perfectly happily — a key that cannot do the one thing it was made for, and nothing on the screen to say so.

A test that has to see hydration happen

The obvious hook was the wrong one. An afterNavigate of type enter is SvelteKit’s own word for “the app has hydrated”, and the first version of this marker used it. The marker then appeared on the settings page and on no other. enter goes out once, a moment after hydration starts, to whichever callbacks are registered by then. afterNavigate registers in onMount, and on a page that awaits a query as it hydrates, with no pending snippet to stand in for it, the layout does not mount until that await has resolved. Three of the four workspace pages do, and the marker never appeared on them. onMount has no event to miss. So the marker has a test of its own, on all four workspace pages, checking both sides: absent while the bundle is held, present once it is let through.

The form test holds the client bundle back, types and chooses while the page is only the server’s HTML, then lets the bundle through. It checks the marker on both sides — absent while it types, so it cannot accidentally type after hydration and prove nothing; present before it looks, so it cannot pass by looking before hydration had a chance to throw anything away — and then reads the key list the form’s own refresh brought back, so the scope it finds is the one the server stored. Its twin on the explore page saves a view and finds it listed under the name typed early.

A list that redraws without a reload

That test used to reload the page before it read the list, and the reload was covering for a bug. Every form on this page refreshes the list it changed, in the same request: the handler calls keys({ tenant }).refresh(), and the new rows come back with the result. The page then drew the old ones. A key that had just been made was missing from the list, a revoked key still offered to be revoked, and a removed view stayed where it was. A reload put all three right, which is why nothing had noticed.

Both lists were drawn with {#await keys(…) then list}. A throwaway page that read the same query four ways settled what was wrong. When the form came back, the {#await} block did run again, and it resolved with the rows from before the refresh. query.current, a bare {await …} and an await held in a {@const} all showed the new rows. One more result explains why the fix removes the block rather than adding something next to it: with an {#await} on the same query in the same boundary, an await beside it went stale too.

The console had said so at every stale read, in one line: Svelte’s derived_inert warning, “reading a derived belonging to a now-destroyed effect may result in stale values”. A query keeps its rows in $derived values, and the block was reading them after they had stopped updating. The old page printed it when a key was created and again when one was revoked; the new page prints nothing.

The page holds the rows in {const list = $derived(await …)} rather than in a {@const}, because the Svelte documentation now calls the older tag legacy: “{@const x = y} is legacy syntax — use {const x = $derived(y)} instead”. An await in the markup is also what the remote-functions documentation reaches for first: “while using await is recommended, as an alternative the query also has loading, error and current properties”.

Two states that never ran

The blocks had a second fault, and it had been in plain view the whole time. Each list sits in a <svelte:boundary> with a pending snippet and a failed snippet, and in the browser neither one ever ran. A boundary waits for await expressions. Its pending snippet “will be shown when the boundary is first created, and will remain visible until all the await expressions inside the boundary have resolved”, and an {#await} block is not an await expression. It is a block that branches “on the three possible states of a Promise”, and these blocks had only the then branch.

So the server drew “Loading…”, because during server-side rendering a boundary with a pending snippet renders that snippet. Then the page hydrated and the block put nothing in its place. A list that was slow showed a blank space, and a list that failed stayed blank, with nothing in the console either. An await puts both states back. “Errors in await expressions will bubble to the nearest error boundary”, and the remote-functions documentation says the same of a query: “until the promise resolves — and if it errors — the nearest <svelte:boundary> will be invoked.”

When the failed snippet finally ran, it showed one more mistake. The keys’ snippet looked for the server’s message on error.body, which is where an HttpError keeps it, and found nothing there. The boundary is not handed the error that was thrown. Svelte’s mount and hydrate take a transformError function that “transforms a render-time error before it is passed to a failed snippet”, and SvelteKit passes one that returns an App.Error. The message is on that object directly.

The same lookup sat in four more boundaries — the traces list, the trace page, the drawer and the alerts page — and each showed its fallback sentence whatever the server had said. The views’ snippet did not look at the error at all and had one sentence for every failure. All of them read message now, with no fallback, because every error a boundary is handed has been through handleError and has one. A command’s rejection is the exception, and the remote-functions chapter shows both shapes side by side.

Tests for the lists

The tests that change a list mark the document before they submit and check the mark afterwards. A list can come out right because the page was rendered again: a reload does that, and so does a click that lands before hydration and posts the form the old-fashioned way. Either one replaces the document and takes the mark with it, so neither can pass for a list that redrew in place.

The other two are about the states, and both look only after hydration, because the server’s HTML shows “Loading…” whatever the browser goes on to do. The first holds both list requests back and expects the live page to say it is loading. Then it lets the requests through and expects the rows. Holding a request is the same small helper the explore tests use, and two matchers say which requests to hold.

The second needs the server to refuse for real, so it ends the session between the page and its rows. The page is drawn signed in. The bundle is held while the cookie is cleared, and the lists are then asked for with no cookie at all. Both lists’ failed snippets must show the server’s own words, which is also the check that catches an error.body lookup, or a fixed sentence in its place.

Five claims, on both viewports, and each fails on its own assertion. The revoke test makes its key and then opens the page from scratch, so it is about the revoke alone and not about the list that creating the key should have refreshed. The reload in the hydration test was then removed, because without it that test still checks what it always did — the scope the server stored — and now fails on the old page as well.

Checkpoint

  • A key is displayed once and never again.
  • A revoked key still appears, marked, with who made it and when.
  • A saved view of "the last hour" means the last hour tomorrow.
  • A name and a scope chosen before the page hydrates are the ones the key is minted with.
  • A view name typed before the explore page hydrates is the name it is saved under.
  • A new key is listed, a revoked one says so, and a removed view is gone — all without a reload.
  • While a list loads it says so, and when it cannot load it says why.
